planting.note: Divide and repot in a fine bark-and-sphagnum mix in warm, deep shade, keeping the roots evenly moist year-round without letting the mix go soggy.

directions: Pot in a well-draining mix of fine fir bark, perlite, and sphagnum moss, and grow in warm, shaded conditions that mimic the humid forest floor of Vietnam, Thailand, and Cambodia where this species naturally grows among leaf litter. Each fan of mottled, strap-shaped leaves sends up a single wiry stem bearing one long-lasting flower at a time, with a coral-pink dorsal sepal and twisted green-and-maroon petals. Keep the roots evenly moist without ever letting the mix turn soggy, and maintain warmth above 60°F even on winter nights. It reblooms reliably under the same steady warm shade it receives all year, without needing the pronounced seasonal light or temperature shift many other slipper orchids require.

planting.note: Mount or pot divisions so the long pendulous petals can hang freely over the container edge, and grow in warm, humid, bright shade.

directions: This Borneo native is famous for producing the longest petals of any orchid, with ribbon-like, twisted olive-and-maroon petals that can trail two to three feet below the flower. In the wild it clings to limestone cliff faces in Sarawak in constant humid shade, so in cultivation it does best in a hanging basket or raised pot that lets the petals drape downward unobstructed. Use a coarse, fast-draining bark mix, water generously but let the mix approach dryness between waterings, and provide warm, bright shade rather than direct sun. Because wild populations are extremely limited and heavily protected, nearly all plants in cultivation come from artificially propagated divisions or seedlings, not wild collection.

planting.note: Grow divisions in a small pot of fine bark mix under cooler, filtered shade than most slipper orchids, since this is a cool-intermediate grower.

directions: Unlike many slipper orchids, this species has plain mid-green leaves without mottling, and its single flower is covered in dense, bristly hairs along the twisted apple-green and maroon-purple petals, giving the species its name. Found on mossy banks and limestone outcrops across the eastern Himalaya, Yunnan, and northern Vietnam, it prefers cooler nights than lowland Paphiopedilum species and can suffer in constant tropical warmth. Keep it in a small pot of fine bark mix, moist but never waterlogged, in bright shade with good air movement. A noticeable winter temperature drop helps trigger the spring flush of flowers.

planting.note: Pot small divisions in a fine, fast-draining limestone-friendly bark mix and grow in cool, bright shade with a noticeable winter temperature drop.

directions: A relatively recently described species from limestone karst along the China-Vietnam border, this compact Paphiopedilum forms a tight rosette of mottled leaves and carries a single rounded, pouch-shaped flower in warm tan and maroon tones. It grows at higher elevation than many of its lowland relatives, so it appreciates cooler nights and benefits from a distinct winter temperature dip to initiate flower spikes. Pot in a fine, fast-draining bark mix and keep evenly moist but never waterlogged, since the species naturally roots into mossy limestone crevices with sharp drainage. Its compact size makes it well suited to windowsill growing where larger slipper orchids would not fit.

planting.note: Grow divisions in a limestone-chip-and-bark mix in cool, bright shade, and check midday for the species' distinctive fragrance when flowers are fresh.

directions: One of the few genuinely fragrant slipper orchids, this Yunnan, China native produces pale yellow-green flowers with a sweet scent most noticeable around midday, held above a rosette of softly mottled leaves. It naturally grows rooted into limestone cliff crevices in cool, deeply shaded ravine forest, so in cultivation it wants a mineral-rich, fast-draining mix with added limestone chips and a cool-intermediate temperature range rather than constant tropical warmth. Keep the compost evenly moist and never let it dry out completely, since the species has no pseudobulbs to store reserves. Good air movement around the foliage helps prevent the rot this species can be prone to in stagnant humidity.

planting.note: Mount divisions on bark or pot in coarse orchid mix, water and feed heavily through the growing season, then withhold water almost entirely once canes mature for winter.

directions: This Himalayan-foothill-to-Southeast-Asia species produces tall, cane-like deciduous stems that drop their leaves before flowering, then burst into clusters of golden-orange blooms with a deeply fringed, ruffled lip along the bare canes in late winter and spring. Grow it in bright, filtered light rather than deep shade, water and fertilize generously during the warm growing season to build thick canes, then cut back sharply on water once growth stops and the leaves fall, since a cool, dry winter rest is essential for triggering bloom. Mount it on a slab or pot it in a coarse, fast-draining bark mix that dries quickly between waterings. Skipping the dry rest is the most common reason growers get lush canes but no flowers.

planting.note: Grow in a hanging basket so the long pendulous canes can arch downward, in warm, filtered light with a brief cooler dry spell after the canes mature.

directions: Native to the lower Himalayan foothills, India, and mainland Southeast Asia, this species sends up long, pendulous canes that are best grown in a hanging basket or mounted slab where they can arch freely. Its soft yellow flowers, marked with maroon blotches deep in the throat, carry a distinctive musky fragrance that gives the species its name and is most noticeable in warm midday air. Water and feed well through the warm growing season, then allow a brief cooler, drier spell after the canes finish maturing to encourage the following season's flower buds. Provide bright, filtered light rather than dense shade, since too little light produces long canes but few flowers.

planting.note: Pot divisions in coarse bark, water heavily in summer to build canes, then give a pronounced cool, dry winter rest to force the spring bloom.

directions: Found at cooler, higher elevations across the eastern Himalaya, Myanmar, and southern China, this deciduous-cane species produces large, waxy, fragrant white flowers with vivid magenta petal tips and a deep maroon-and-gold blotch in the throat, borne along leafless canes in late winter. It demands a more pronounced cool, dry winter rest than many of its lowland relatives; without several weeks of cooler nights and minimal water after the canes mature, plants often decline to flower. Grow in bright, filtered light during the growing season, water and feed generously to bulk up the canes, and pot in a coarse, fast-draining bark mix. The strong fragrance and large flower size make it one of the more dramatic cool-growing deciduous dendrobiums for a bright sunroom or greenhouse.

planting.note: Plant offshoots in pure long-fiber sphagnum moss kept standing in a tray of distilled or rain water, and keep well out of direct sun.

directions: Unlike most sundews, which sprawl in open, sun-baked bogs, this species is restricted to the deep shade of rainforest floor leaf litter on a handful of mountains in far north Queensland, Australia. Its broad, flat, fan-shaped leaves are covered in short sticky hairs rather than the long glandular tentacles typical of the genus, and it tolerates far less light than almost any other Drosera in cultivation, scorching badly if exposed to direct sun. Grow it in pure long-fiber sphagnum moss or a peat-and-perlite mix kept constantly wet with rain or distilled water, in warm, humid, low-light conditions such as a covered terrarium. It spreads slowly by producing small plantlets at the base of mature rosettes, which can be separated and potted on once rooted.
